roof_pitch.rule: Pitch is set by the roofing material and the local precipitation regime, not by a fixed style number, and both members independently state the same two-band split.

pitch_snow_dominant.note: scandinavian-log-vernacular.c04: sod roofs 22-30 degrees. swiss-chalet.c04 / defining_characteristics: 18-25 degrees in the high alps. Union given here.

pitch_rain_or_shingle.note: Both members give the identical figure independently: scandinavian-log-vernacular's split-shingle roofs run 35-45 degrees, and swiss-chalet's lower-valley/Mittelland roofs run 35-45 degrees. The one numeric coincidence in this kit not manufactured by rounding a shared range — both sources state 35-45 verbatim.

wing_strategy.rule: A log wall cannot be lengthened once built. The household or farm grows by adding a pen, stacking a storey, or adding a wholly separate building — never by extending one wall.

growth_unit.note: EDITORIAL, AND NO SOURCE IS RECORDED (OQ 18, annotated 25 Aug 2026; reclassified 25 Aug after audit). The basis stated for this slot is: "A log wall cannot be lengthened once built. The household or farm grows by adding a pen, stacking a storey, or adding a wholly separate building — never by extending one wall." -- which is the reasoning, not a citation. A CATEGORICAL CALL, NOT A MEASUREMENT -- it names a treatment or a class, so no citation would sharpen it into a number. What it needs is a source showing the tradition makes this choice, not a figure.

wing_strategy.note: Both members' own hard constraints use almost identical wording: scandinavian-log-vernacular.c01 ('No log wall may exceed about 9 m without an intersecting cross-wall... the building grows by adding pens, storeys or separate buildings; a wall cannot simply be made longer') and swiss-chalet.c01 ('No log wall may exceed about 9 m ... the type grows by stacking storeys or adding a separate building, never by lengthening a wall').

packs.note: log-module's own wing_strategy derived_rule states the identical mechanism ('You cannot make a pen bigger... a household that needs more room builds another pen') and is bound at expression=module, i.e. the log-length ceiling itself. Numeric calibration (12-18 ft) is American/Upland-South; both Nordic and Alpine members independently state a slightly longer 6-9 m (20-30 ft) ceiling in their own text, so use this pack for the generative mechanism, not its numeric band.

construction_type.rule: Solid horizontally-stacked, corner-notched log wall (Blockbau/laft) with no frame at all — the family's single defining construction fact.
construction_type.note: Both members' own text states this identically and cross-references the other: swiss-chalet's distinguished_from entry for scandinavian-log-vernacular opens 'Both are Blockbau, and they share the log-length constraint and the settlement problem.'

packs.note: log-module's own applies_to list names nordic-alpine-vernacular directly, alongside both scandinavian-log-vernacular and swiss-chalet by id — the one pack in the corpus explicitly scoped to this family as a whole, not just judgment-bound to it.

primary_cladding.rule: The structural log wall is left exposed as the finished wall in both traditions; nothing is applied over it as siding. (Finish differs — see color_strategy.)

foundation_expression.rule: The bottom (sill) log sits clear of grade on a stone base — pads, a dry-laid footing, or the uphill grade itself — and is never in contact with soil.

clearance.note: scandinavian-log-vernacular.c03 states this explicitly and numerically: sill log on stone pads at least 300 mm clear of grade, treated as a sacrificial course. swiss-chalet.c04 states the same categorical rule ('must sit on a masonry base or on the uphill grade, never on the ground') without a number; the upper end of the range is not independently sourced for the chalet and is carried here by analogy to the same structural logic, not a chalet-specific figure.

packs.note: log-module's own foundation_expression rule (pier height, part * 1.5, 18 in typical) is calibrated to the American Upland-South pier-and-crawlspace system, a different assembly from a Nordic/Alpine stone-pad or masonry base — cited for the shared underlying principle (never let the sill touch grade), not for its specific 18 in figure.

corner_quoin.rule: The corner is a visible, projecting, notched log joint — not a masonry quoin — in both traditions. The specific notch profile is regional and is not shared across the family.
corner_quoin.note: scandinavian-log-vernacular names several regional notch profiles (findal, dovetail, round, square) as 'regional signatures as reliable as an accent.' swiss-chalet's own text does not name a specific profile but its diagnostic_tells state 'log courses visibly continuous across the whole wall, with the corner notching exposed and projecting at the corners' — the same generic condition. The profile itself is left open, correctly, at the family level.

packs.note: log-module's own corner_quoin derived rules (projection ~0.75 x part, notch depth ~40% of log thickness) are calibrated to the American Upland-South notch band and are not re-derived here for the Nordic/Alpine scale, but the mechanism — the overhang and the notch depth ratio being the diagnostic detail of the whole craft — transfers directly.

color_strategy.rule: The family splits into exactly two documented, mutually exclusive finishes, and both members' own texts name the contrast explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

variants.note: swiss-chalet: timber left bare; 'the sun-blackened larch of a two-hundred-year-old south face is the finest weathering material in Europe.' Its own constraint c05 keeps ornament off the log wall itself.
scandinavian-log-vernacular: Falu red from the 18th century onward, with white lead trim at the windows, applied 'to the whole cluster or none of it' (c05, soft). Not used before ~1700.

color_strategy.note: swiss-chalet's own distinguished_from entry states the contrast directly: 'The chalet leaves timber bare; the Nordic farm paints it red.'

window_surround_wood.rule: No applied moulded architrave or casing — the log ends themselves form the jamb, with a settlement gap above the head, in both traditions.
window_surround_wood.note: scandinavian-log-vernacular.c02 and swiss-chalet.c02 both require a settlement gap above every opening head with no rigid element passing through the wall without a slip joint. This is the same principle log-module's own window_surround_wood rule states for the American branch of the same construction system ('no architrave, no backband and no casing on the outside of a log wall').

packs.note: log-module explicitly names applying a moulded surround to a log building as 'the commonest single error in log revival work' — the same warning applies directly to both Nordic and Alpine work.

window_grouping_rule.rule: Openings are small and few, sized and placed to interrupt as few log courses as possible; a large or ribboned opening is structurally impossible in a solid log wall.
window_grouping_rule.note: scandinavian-log-vernacular: 'There is no bay rhythm. Openings are cut where the room needs them, few and small.' swiss-chalet: openings 'must be small and grouped, because each one interrupts the continuity of the courses' — chalet additionally organises its small openings into a banded Fensterband (three to six lights), which is NOT independently attested for the Nordic branch and is left as a chalet-specific refinement, not asserted here at family level.

packs.note: log-module's window_grouping_rule derived rule (max opening width ~42 in on its own American calibration) states the identical mechanism — every opening cuts the wall logs and load has to arch over the gap — but its numeric ceiling is not re-derived here for the Nordic/Alpine scale.

order.rule: No classical order or apparatus in either member. All ornament in this family is carved/sawn vernacular carpentry (bargeboard, purlin ends, gallery balustrades, inscription bands) concentrated on the gable, not an order-derived vocabulary.

balustrade.note: swiss-chalet's Lauben galleries do carry real 'sawn or turned balustrades,' and scandinavian-log-vernacular's raised stabbur/loft carries a comparable carved gallery — but both are vernacular carpentry railings, not a classical/order-derived balustrade, and they attach to different elements (an integral gallery on the main dwelling for the chalet; a subsidiary storehouse for the Nordic farm). Forbidden here in the classical-apparatus sense; a style-level kit should record the real railings via porch_rail instead, which this family kit deliberately leaves open given how differently the two members deploy it.
